title: Geometry of a monomial trait model with a generically invertible exponent
statement:
A trait is $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $R$ a Noetherian local domain of dimension one and principal maximal ideal; a uniformizer $\pi$ generates that maximal ideal. Let $n\geq1$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbf N$, with at least one $a_i$ nonzero and invertible in the fraction field $K$ of $R$. Put
$$B=R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/(\prod_i T_i^{a_i}-\pi).$$
Then $B$ is a Noetherian integral domain and a regular ring [def-weil-regular-scheme, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], and $\operatorname{Spec}B\to S$ has smooth generic fibre [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Zero exponents are allowed. Polynomial rings and spectra mean [def-weil-polynomial-ring, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. No excellence or henselianity assumption is made.

proof.text: Write $P=R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]$, $M=\prod_iT_i^{a_i}$ and $f=M-\pi$. The hypotheses on the trait and [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] identify $R$ as a DVR, hence a principal ideal domain. Also $R$ is regular local directly from its dimension one and its one-generator maximal ideal. Its only primes are $(0)$ and its maximal ideal: a strictly intermediate prime would give a chain of length two. The localization at $(0)$ is its fraction field, regular local of dimension zero. Thus $R$ is a regular ring.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250-251; assertion (i) is left as an exercise. The following is an agent-written solution.

proof.text: By [lem-trf-polynomial-ring-regular-base], $P$ is regular and in particular Noetherian. The quotient $B=P/(f)$ is Noetherian: an ideal of $B$ is the image of its inverse-image ideal of $P$, and the images of finite generators generate it. This uses exactly the finite-generation definition of Noetherianity.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250-251; assertion (i) is left as an exercise. The following is an agent-written solution.

proof.text:
Choose $j$ with $a_j>0$, put $A=R[T_i:i
e j]$, $d=a_j$, and $u=\prod_{i
e j}T_i^{a_i}$. Regard $f$ as $uX^d-\pi\in A[X]$. By [lem-per-polynomial-ufd-prime-quotient], $A$ and $P$ are UFDs. The ideal $\mathfrak p=\pi A$ is prime since $A/\pi A=(R/\pi R)[T_i:i
e j]$ is a polynomial domain. In particular $\pi$ is a prime element of $A$. The monomial $u$ is nonzero modulo $\pi$, and $\pi
otin\pi^2A$: comparing constant coefficients would otherwise give $1\in\pi R$ after cancellation in $R$. A common divisor of $u$ and $\pi$ is a unit: a nonunit divisor of the prime element $\pi$ is associated to $\pi$, which cannot divide $u$. Thus $uX^d-\pi$ is primitive. Its lower coefficients are zero except $-\pi$, its leading coefficient is outside $\mathfrak p$, and its constant coefficient is outside $\mathfrak p^2$. The Eisenstein criterion makes $f$ irreducible. The prime-quotient clause of [lem-per-polynomial-ufd-prime-quotient] now makes $B$ an integral domain.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250-251; assertion (i) is left as an exercise. The following is an agent-written solution.

proof.text: Its generic fibre has coordinate ring $C=K[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/(f)$. Choose $j$ for which $a_j>0$ is invertible in $K$. In $C$, $M=\pi$ is a unit. Every $T_i$ with $a_i>0$ is therefore a unit. The formal derivative $D_j(f)=a_jT_j^{a_j-1}\prod_{i\ne j}T_i^{a_i}$ is a unit in $C$, since $T_jD_j(f)=a_j\pi$. This formula follows by the monomial rule in [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]; variables of exponent zero contribute the factor $1$.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250-251; assertion (i) is left as an exercise. The following is an agent-written solution.

proof.text: The generic fibre is smooth by the lifting definition [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Indeed $C$ is finitely presented. For a square-zero ideal $J\subset D$ in any $K$-algebra and a map $C\to D/J$, lift the coordinate images to $t_i\in D$. Then $f(t)\in J$ and $v=D_j(f)(t)$ is a unit: a lift of an inverse modulo $J$ gives a product $1+e$, $e\in J$, whose inverse is $1-e$. Keep all coordinates except $j$ fixed and replace $t_j$ by $t_j-f(t)v^{-1}$. Polynomial expansion, with all terms of degree at least two in $J$ zero, gives $f(t)-v f(t)v^{-1}=0$. This defines a lift $C\to D$. These maps are precisely the required lifts for affine first-order thickenings, so formal smoothness and finite presentation give smoothness.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250-251; assertion (i) is left as an exercise. The following is an agent-written solution.

proof.text: For regularity take a prime $q\subset P$ containing $f$, set $L=P_q$ and $\mathfrak m=qL$. It is regular local by the regularity of $P$. If $\pi\notin q$, then $q\cap R=(0)$ (the only other prime of $R$ contains $\pi$), so all nonzero elements of $R$ are invertible in $L$. Hence $L$ is also the localization of $K[T_1,\ldots,T_n]$ at the extended prime, and $L/(f)$ is a prime localization of $C$. The polynomial ring over the field $K$ is regular by [lem-trf-polynomial-ring-regular-base]. Step 4 supplies a derivation with unit image on $f$, so [lem-weil-pbc-hypersurface-derivation-regular] says $C$ is regular. Consequently $L/(f)$ is regular local.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250-251; assertion (i) is left as an exercise. The following is an agent-written solution.

proof.text: Now suppose $\pi\in q$. The ring $L/(\pi)$ is the localization of $(R/\pi R)[T_1,\ldots,T_n]$ at the prime induced by $q$, hence regular local by [lem-trf-polynomial-ring-regular-base]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-regular-local-quotient-independent-generators] to the ideal $I=(\pi)$ in the regular local ring $L$. It gives generators of $I$ with independent classes in $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. If $\pi\in\mathfrak m^2$, all these classes would be zero, forcing the generating set to be empty, hence $I=0$. This is impossible: $P$ is a polynomial domain over $R$, and its localization at a prime keeps the nonzero element $\pi$ nonzero. Therefore $\pi\notin\mathfrak m^2$.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250-251; assertion (i) is left as an exercise. The following is an agent-written solution.

proof.text: Let $I_q=\{i:a_i>0,\ T_i\in q\}$. It is nonempty, since $M=f+\pi\in q$ and $q$ is prime. Set $r=\sum_{i\in I_q}a_i$. If $r\ge2$, then $M\in\mathfrak m^2$ and $f=M-\pi\notin\mathfrak m^2$ by Step 7. If $r=1$, then $I_q=\{i\}$ and $a_i=1$. Write $M=wT_i$, where $w$ is independent of $T_i$ and is a unit in $L$ because all its factors are outside $q$. Extend the partial derivative $D_i$ to $L$ by $D_i(a/s)=(sD_i(a)-aD_i(s))/s^2$. Then $D_i(f)=w$ is a unit. The Leibniz rule gives $D_i(\mathfrak m^2)\subseteq\mathfrak m$, so again $f\notin\mathfrak m^2$. In both cases the regular local hypersurface criterion gives $L/(f)$ regular local. These are exactly the remaining prime localizations of $B$; with Step 2 this proves that $B$ is regular.
